A Cynical Ploy to Block California’s Wealth Tax
Some voters who support the proposal might be duped into nullifying it.
By Marc Novicoff (https://www.theatlantic.com/author/marc-novicoff/)
Illustration by Adam Maida / The Atlantic
October 30, 2026
Share
Save
Listen − 1.0 x +
Seek
0:00 6:22
The most important decision facing California voters this year is not which candidates to support for higher office, but whether to approve a wealth tax on the state’s approximately 250 billionaires. The ballot initiative that would impose the tax has plenty of enemies, among not only the superrich but also the many Californians, including Governor Gavin Newsom, who worry about losing the superrich to other states. But thanks to a deviously cynical electoral maneuver by the measure’s opponents, the people who ultimately doom it might include some of those who vote for it.
Proposition 40 was spearheaded by Dave Regan, who leads California’s large and powerful health-care workers’ union, in response to the Medicaid cuts in Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act. If approved, the initiative would create a onetime 5 percent tax on all billionaire wealth, and the proceeds—perhaps as much as $100 billion—would be earmarked mostly for state health-care spending. To make sure the superrich don’t flee before they can be taxed, the policy would apply retroactively to anyone who lived in the state at the start of 2026.
Predictably, some of the billionaires in question are seeking to defeat the initiative. The Google co-founder Sergey Brin preemptively moved his residence and businesses to Nevada in 2025 and seeded the new political organization Building a Better California with $102 million from his stash. (That might sound like a lot, but the tax would have cost him about $12 billion.) Thanks to the donations of other tech tycoons, the group has raised more than $333 million in total.
Read: If you tax them, will they leave? (https://www.theatlantic.com/economy/2026/01/california-wealth-tax-billionaire-migration/685779/)
Plan A is to convince voters that Proposition 40 is unwise via a barrage of TV and social-media ads. In case that doesn’t work, the opponents have come up with Plans B and C: Propositions 41 and 42. These initiatives take advantage of a feature of California law: If two conflicting ballot measures pass in the same election, the one with more votes prevails. On the surface, both look innocuous and unrelated to the wealth tax. Proposition 41 is being pitched as a fiscal-responsibility measure, and Proposition 42 is ostensibly about protecting voters’ retirement savings. But the initiatives are designed to directly conflict with the wealth-tax measure. Proposition 41 would institute audit requirements for new special taxes and void any programs that are exempt from the state’s existing spending limit, which the new wealth tax would be. Proposition 42 would prohibit both retroactive taxes and any taxes on non-real-estate property, each of which describes Proposition 40.
This tactic is completely legal, and efforts to change the rules could have unfortunate downstream consequences. For instance, if counterproposals were disallowed, then a group that caught wind of an upcoming initiative could block it simply by being the first to gather enough signatures. Still, the rule can, perversely, lead to antimajoritarian outcomes by preventing proposals supported by more than half of the population from becoming law if another proposal on the ballot happens to, or is designed to, negate it.
Propositions 41 and 42 also take advantage of the possibility that voters will not realize that the measures conflict, and will vote yes on more than one of them. They might think that audits are sensible and that spending limits should be observed, or that personal property such as cars and engagement rings and 401(k)s shouldn’t be taxed, and fail to understand that these principles stand in the way of their belief that billionaires ought to pay a wealth tax.
Other voters might prefer audits to a wealth tax even though they’d be perfectly fine with both; in that sense, the countermeasure forces them to choose between two policies that could coexist. Still other voters are likely to be overwhelmed or annoyed by having to parse so many measures and decide to oppose all of them: Political scientists have found that the longer the ballot, the more likely people are to vote no.
Read: The one tax the rich can’t escape (https://www.theatlantic.com/ideas/2026/05/mamdani-property-tax-new-york/687031/)
Historically, Californians are not easily fooled by this type of gamesmanship. But in a close contest, only a small subset of voters needs to fit into the above categories for the countermeasure strategy to work. Imagine that 51 percent of voters want a wealth tax and 49 percent oppose it. If all of those who oppose it vote for Proposition 41, knowing that the measure will negate Proposition 40, and just 3 percent of the electorate votes for both, then Proposition 41 will pass with 52 percent of the vote, nullifying the wealth tax that 51 percent of Californians voted to approve.
Polls indicate that this outcome is possible. A September survey by the Public Policy Institute of California had the wealth tax passing 52–46, Proposition 41 passing 51–44, and Proposition 42 passing 54–43, which would result in only Proposition 42 (the one about taxing property) going into effect. (A more recent poll (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/) by the same organization showed the wealth tax at only 46 percent support.) A poll from UC Berkeley found that a larger slice of the electorate was undecided about the countermeasures than about Proposition 40, suggesting that some voters don’t realize the measures conflict.
At the turn of the 20th century, many western-state legislatures were captured by the owners of local railroad and mining monopolies. Progressives and populists introduced ballot measures as a way to circumvent those plutocrats and return power to the people. But, as the fight over Proposition 40 shows, that works only if voters can withstand plutocrats’ efforts to capture the ballot-measure process too.

A Cynical Ploy to Block California’s Wealth Tax
Some voters who support the proposal might be duped into nullifying it.
By Marc Novicoff (https://www.theatlantic.com/author/marc-novicoff/)
Illustration by Adam Maida / The Atlantic
October 30, 2026
Share
Save
Listen − 1.0 x +
Seek
0:00 6:22
The most important decision facing California voters this year is not which candidates to support for higher office, but whether to approve a wealth tax on the state’s approximately 250 billionaires. The ballot initiative that would impose the tax has plenty of enemies, among not only the superrich but also the many Californians, including Governor Gavin Newsom, who worry about losing the superrich to other states. But thanks to a deviously cynical electoral maneuver by the measure’s opponents, the people who ultimately doom it might include some of those who vote for it.
Proposition 40 was spearheaded by Dave Regan, who leads California’s large and powerful health-care workers’ union, in response to the Medicaid cuts in Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act. If approved, the initiative would create a onetime 5 percent tax on all billionaire wealth, and the proceeds—perhaps as much as $100 billion—would be earmarked mostly for state health-care spending. To make sure the superrich don’t flee before they can be taxed, the policy would apply retroactively to anyone who lived in the state at the start of 2026.
Predictably, some of the billionaires in question are seeking to defeat the initiative. The Google co-founder Sergey Brin preemptively moved his residence and businesses to Nevada in 2025 and seeded the new political organization Building a Better California with $102 million from his stash. (That might sound like a lot, but the tax would have cost him about $12 billion.) Thanks to the donations of other tech tycoons, the group has raised more than $333 million in total.
Read: If you tax them, will they leave? (https://www.theatlantic.com/economy/2026/01/california-wealth-tax-billionaire-migration/685779/)
Plan A is to convince voters that Proposition 40 is unwise via a barrage of TV and social-media ads. In case that doesn’t work, the opponents have come up with Plans B and C: Propositions 41 and 42. These initiatives take advantage of a feature of California law: If two conflicting ballot measures pass in the same election, the one with more votes prevails. On the surface, both look innocuous and unrelated to the wealth tax. Proposition 41 is being pitched as a fiscal-responsibility measure, and Proposition 42 is ostensibly about protecting voters’ retirement savings. But the initiatives are designed to directly conflict with the wealth-tax measure. Proposition 41 would institute audit requirements for new special taxes and void any programs that are exempt from the state’s existing spending limit, which the new wealth tax would be. Proposition 42 would prohibit both retroactive taxes and any taxes on non-real-estate property, each of which describes Proposition 40.
This tactic is completely legal, and efforts to change the rules could have unfortunate downstream consequences. For instance, if counterproposals were disallowed, then a group that caught wind of an upcoming initiative could block it simply by being the first to gather enough signatures. Still, the rule can, perversely, lead to antimajoritarian outcomes by preventing proposals supported by more than half of the population from becoming law if another proposal on the ballot happens to, or is designed to, negate it.
Propositions 41 and 42 also take advantage of the possibility that voters will not realize that the measures conflict, and will vote yes on more than one of them. They might think that audits are sensible and that spending limits should be observed, or that personal property such as cars and engagement rings and 401(k)s shouldn’t be taxed, and fail to understand that these principles stand in the way of their belief that billionaires ought to pay a wealth tax.
Other voters might prefer audits to a wealth tax even though they’d be perfectly fine with both; in that sense, the countermeasure forces them to choose between two policies that could coexist. Still other voters are likely to be overwhelmed or annoyed by having to parse so many measures and decide to oppose all of them: Political scientists have found that the longer the ballot, the more likely people are to vote no.
Read: The one tax the rich can’t escape (https://www.theatlantic.com/ideas/2026/05/mamdani-property-tax-new-york/687031/)
Historically, Californians are not easily fooled by this type of gamesmanship. But in a close contest, only a small subset of voters needs to fit into the above categories for the countermeasure strategy to work. Imagine that 51 percent of voters want a wealth tax and 49 percent oppose it. If all of those who oppose it vote for Proposition 41, knowing that the measure will negate Proposition 40, and just 3 percent of the electorate votes for both, then Proposition 41 will pass with 52 percent of the vote, nullifying the wealth tax that 51 percent of Californians voted to approve.
Polls indicate that this outcome is possible. A September survey by the Public Policy Institute of California had the wealth tax passing 52–46, Proposition 41 passing 51–44, and Proposition 42 passing 54–43, which would result in only Proposition 42 (the one about taxing property) going into effect. (A more recent poll (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/) by the same organization showed the wealth tax at only 46 percent support.) A poll from UC Berkeley found that a larger slice of the electorate was undecided about the countermeasures than about Proposition 40, suggesting that some voters don’t realize the measures conflict.
At the turn of the 20th century, many western-state legislatures were captured by the owners of local railroad and mining monopolies. Progressives and populists introduced ballot measures as a way to circumvent those plutocrats and return power to the people. But, as the fight over Proposition 40 shows, that works only if voters can withstand plutocrats’ efforts to capture the ballot-measure process too.

For instance, if counterproposals were disallowed, then a group that caught wind of an upcoming initiative could block it simply by being the first to gather enough signatures. Still, the rule can, perversely, lead to antimajoritarian outcomes by preventing proposals supported by more than half of the population from becoming law if another proposal on the ballot happens to, or is designed to, negate it.
Propositions 41 and 42 also take advantage of the possibility that voters will not realize that the measures conflict, and will vote yes on more than one of them. They might think that audits are sensible and that spending limits should be observed, or that personal property such as cars and engagement rings and 401(k)s shouldn’t be taxed, and fail to understand that these principles stand in the way of their belief that billionaires ought to pay a wealth tax.
Other voters might prefer audits to a wealth tax even though they’d be perfectly fine with both; in that sense, the countermeasure forces them to choose between two policies that could coexist. Still other voters are likely to be overwhelmed or annoyed by having to parse so many measures and decide to oppose all of them: Political scientists have found that the longer the ballot, the more likely people are to vote no.
Read: The one tax the rich can’t escape (https://www.theatlantic.com/ideas/2026/05/mamdani-property-tax-new-york/687031/)
Historically, Californians are not easily fooled by this type of gamesmanship. But in a close contest, only a small subset of voters needs to fit into the above categories for the countermeasure strategy to work. Imagine that 51 percent of voters want a wealth tax and 49 percent oppose it. If all of those who oppose it vote for Proposition 41, knowing that the measure will negate Proposition 40, and just 3 percent of the electorate votes for both, then Proposition 41 will pass with 52 percent of the vote, nullifying the wealth tax that 51 percent of Californians voted to approve.
Polls indicate that this outcome is possible. A September survey by the Public Policy Institute of California had the wealth tax passing 52–46, Proposition 41 passing 51–44, and Proposition 42 passing 54–43, which would result in only Proposition 42 (the one about taxing property) going into effect. (A more recent poll (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/) by the same organization showed the wealth tax at only 46 percent support.) A poll from UC Berkeley found that a larger slice of the electorate was undecided about the countermeasures than about Proposition 40, suggesting that some voters don’t realize the measures conflict.
At the turn of the 20th century, many western-state legislatures were captured by the owners of local railroad and mining monopolies. Progressives and populists introduced ballot measures as a way to circumvent those plutocrats and return power to the people. But, as the fight over Proposition 40 shows, that works only if voters can withstand plutocrats’ efforts to capture the ballot-measure process too.

Good — this confirms:
1. The SF Chronicle editorial board (which also opposes Prop 40, or at least is skeptical) recommends NO on Prop 42, calling it a "poison-pill measure" and "appalling tactic." Key points from their editorial:
   - "No one is coming for your 401(k)" — CA follows the federal framework (tax on withdrawal), no concerted efforts to change that.
   - Prop 42 is funded by Brin's PAC.
   - Prop 40 does include one wrinkle: Roth IRAs worth >$10M are counted in taxable wealth — but qualified pensions/401(k)s are excluded. (Interesting nuance: a law professor opposing 42 pointed this out.)
   - All six wealth tax proposals since 2019 died in the legislature without passing.
   - Prop 42's retroactivity ban is unnecessary and could create legal complications vs. the Supreme Court's Carlton standard (retroactive taxes constitutional if supported by legitimate legislative purpose).
   - "If you disagree with Prop 40, you can simply vote no."

2. The wealth tax bills history: AB 2088 (2020, 0.4% annual wealth tax on net worth > $30M — died), AB 259 (2023-24, died), plus a handful of others (the "six proposals since 2019" — these include AB 2088, AB 1253 (income tax on high earners, not wealth), AB 259, and maybe SB 35? / ACA 3, and possibly others). These targeted the wealthy ($30M+, or $1B+), not ordinary retirement accounts. So the pro-42 campaign's claim that these were proposals "that would tax retirement and savings accounts" is technically-true-but-misleading framing: they were wealth taxes on the ultra-wealthy, which would include their investment holdings.

Now let me consider the remaining research:
- PPIC poll on Prop 42 (to understand the landscape, though not strictly needed for my recommendation).
- The LA Times editorial board's formal recommendation on Prop 42 (2026). Skelton's column says No. Let me check if the LAT editorial board also published a formal rec.
- Maybe check the Atlantic piece and Forbes piece in more depth.
- Check CalMatters' voter guide positions on Prop 42 (they usually explain both sides; do they have an editorial? No, CalMatters doesn't endorse, but their coverage is informative).

Also worth checking: whether there are any other notable independent assessments — e.g., the California Budget & Policy Center (left-leaning), the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association (pro-taxpayer), the Chamber of Commerce, and what the official opposition says. And any analysis of legal complications (e.g., conflicts with existing constitutional provisions, the "Article VIII" numbering issue — actually adding an "Article VIII" when there might already be... hmm, actually the California Constitution's Article VIII is "Water and Water Rights"? No, that's Article X. Let me not go down this path; the numbering is a minor drafting oddity — actually wait, current Article VIII doesn't exist; it was repealed in 1972? Actually the old Article VIII was "Education," replaced by Article IX in 1880? Hmm. In the current constitution: Article I Declaration of Rights; II Voting; III State of California; IV Legislative; V Executive; VI Judicial; VII Public Officers and Employees; VIII ??? — I believe there's no Article VIII currently (it was repealed), which is why the drafters could add one. OK minor point.)

Let me check the PPIC poll and LA Times editorial board rec on Prop 42. Also, maybe look at the californiatoday.com guide for the funding details ($112.8M, top contributors: Brin and "L. John..." — let me confirm L. John Doerr) and any additional details on the Yes side's arguments (e.g., Nathan Click is the spokesman).

Also I want to double-check the claim in the pro argument: "In the last few years alone, the Legislature and special interests have introduced six separate proposals that would tax retirement and savings accounts." And the LA Times op-ed says five bills. The SF Chron says all six wealth tax proposals since 2019 died. So the claim has a kernel of truth (wealth tax bills were introduced) but they never came close to passing, and they targeted high net worth, not ordinary savers.

One more angle: the "double taxation" claim. Note: Under current law, when you contribute to a traditional 401(k)/IRA, you get a deduction — the money is NOT taxed when earned. It's taxed when withdrawn (as income). So the pro-42 claim that "you already paid taxes on that money when you earned it" is false for traditional retirement accounts. It's true for Roth accounts (taxed when earned, not when withdrawn) and for regular brokerage savings (already-taxed money). But the claim that savings "sitting in retirement accounts" was already taxed is wrong for most retirement savings. Prop 40 excludes retirement accounts anyway (except the Roth >$10M wrinkle).

Let me also look at the Atlantic article more closely, since it's a well-reasoned national perspective, and check the PPIC poll on 42.

A Cynical Ploy to Block California’s Wealth Tax
Some voters who support the proposal might be duped into nullifying it.
By Marc Novicoff (https://www.theatlantic.com/author/marc-novicoff/)
Illustration by Adam Maida / The Atlantic
October 30, 2026
Share
Save
Listen − 1.0 x +
Seek
0:00 6:22
The most important decision facing California voters this year is not which candidates to support for higher office, but whether to approve a wealth tax on the state’s approximately 250 billionaires. The ballot initiative that would impose the tax has plenty of enemies, among not only the superrich but also the many Californians, including Governor Gavin Newsom, who worry about losing the superrich to other states. But thanks to a deviously cynical electoral maneuver by the measure’s opponents, the people who ultimately doom it might include some of those who vote for it.
Proposition 40 was spearheaded by Dave Regan, who leads California’s large and powerful health-care workers’ union, in response to the Medicaid cuts in Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act. If approved, the initiative would create a onetime 5 percent tax on all billionaire wealth, and the proceeds—perhaps as much as $100 billion—would be earmarked mostly for state health-care spending. To make sure the superrich don’t flee before they can be taxed, the policy would apply retroactively to anyone who lived in the state at the start of 2026.
Predictably, some of the billionaires in question are seeking to defeat the initiative. The Google co-founder Sergey Brin preemptively moved his residence and businesses to Nevada in 2025 and seeded the new political organization Building a Better California with $102 million from his stash. (That might sound like a lot, but the tax would have cost him about $12 billion.) Thanks to the donations of other tech tycoons, the group has raised more than $333 million in total.
Read: If you tax them, will they leave? (https://www.theatlantic.com/economy/2026/01/california-wealth-tax-billionaire-migration/685779/)
Plan A is to convince voters that Proposition 40 is unwise via a barrage of TV and social-media ads. In case that doesn’t work, the opponents have come up with Plans B and C: Propositions 41 and 42. These initiatives take advantage of a feature of California law: If two conflicting ballot measures pass in the same election, the one with more votes prevails. On the surface, both look innocuous and unrelated to the wealth tax. Proposition 41 is being pitched as a fiscal-responsibility measure, and Proposition 42 is ostensibly about protecting voters’ retirement savings. But the initiatives are designed to directly conflict with the wealth-tax measure. Proposition 41 would institute audit requirements for new special taxes and void any programs that are exempt from the state’s existing spending limit, which the new wealth tax would be. Proposition 42 would prohibit both retroactive taxes and any taxes on non-real-estate property, each of which describes Proposition 40.
This tactic is completely legal, and efforts to change the rules could have unfortunate downstream consequences. For instance, if counterproposals were disallowed, then a group that caught wind of an upcoming initiative could block it simply by being the first to gather enough signatures. Still, the rule can, perversely, lead to antimajoritarian outcomes by preventing proposals supported by more than half of the population from becoming law if another proposal on the ballot happens to, or is designed to, negate it.
Propositions 41 and 42 also take advantage of the possibility that voters will not realize that the measures conflict, and will vote yes on more than one of them. They might think that audits are sensible and that spending limits should be observed, or that personal property such as cars and engagement rings and 401(k)s shouldn’t be taxed, and fail to understand that these principles stand in the way of their belief that billionaires ought to pay a wealth tax.
Other voters might prefer audits to a wealth tax even though they’d be perfectly fine with both; in that sense, the countermeasure forces them to choose between two policies that could coexist. Still other voters are likely to be overwhelmed or annoyed by having to parse so many measures and decide to oppose all of them: Political scientists have found that the longer the ballot, the more likely people are to vote no.
Read: The one tax the rich can’t escape (https://www.theatlantic.com/ideas/2026/05/mamdani-property-tax-new-york/687031/)
Historically, Californians are not easily fooled by this type of gamesmanship. But in a close contest, only a small subset of voters needs to fit into the above categories for the countermeasure strategy to work. Imagine that 51 percent of voters want a wealth tax and 49 percent oppose it. If all of those who oppose it vote for Proposition 41, knowing that the measure will negate Proposition 40, and just 3 percent of the electorate votes for both, then Proposition 41 will pass with 52 percent of the vote, nullifying the wealth tax that 51 percent of Californians voted to approve.
Polls indicate that this outcome is possible. A September survey by the Public Policy Institute of California had the wealth tax passing 52–46, Proposition 41 passing 51–44, and Proposition 42 passing 54–43, which would result in only Proposition 42 (the one about taxing property) going into effect. (A more recent poll (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/) by the same organization showed the wealth tax at only 46 percent support.) A poll from UC Berkeley found that a larger slice of the electorate was undecided about the countermeasures than about Proposition 40, suggesting that some voters don’t realize the measures conflict.
At the turn of the 20th century, many western-state legislatures were captured by the owners of local railroad and mining monopolies. Progressives and populists introduced ballot measures as a way to circumvent those plutocrats and return power to the people. But, as the fight over Proposition 40 shows, that works only if voters can withstand plutocrats’ efforts to capture the ballot-measure process too.

Excellent. The Atlantic piece adds crucial detail: Sergey Brin preemptively moved his residence and businesses to Nevada in 2025 — so he's not even a California resident anymore, yet he spent $102M seeding Building a Better California to defeat the tax (which would have cost him ~$12 billion).

Now let me consider the LA Times editorial board's formal recommendation, and maybe look at the Forbes piece. Also, let me verify a couple of additional things:

1. LA Times editorial board on Prop 42 (2026).
2. The California Democratic Party position (opposes 42?) and Republican Party (supports?).
3. Any other notable independent voices — e.g., CalTax (California Taxpayers Association), Chamber, Howard Jarvis.

Also I should double-check the claim that Prop 40 excludes pensions/401(k)s but includes Roth IRAs > $10M — from the SF Chron editorial. That's a nuance: Prop 40 counts "Roth IRAs and substantially similar accounts worth more than $10 million" as assets. So there IS a tiny overlap with "retirement accounts" in Prop 40 — but only for mega-Roths of the ultra-wealthy (like Peter Thiel's $5B Roth). That's about billionaires, not ordinary retirees. The LAO analysis said "Real estate, pensions, and retirement accounts generally would be excluded."

Let me search for the LA Times endorsement on Prop 42 2026.

Proposition 42 says it protects your 401(k). Who does it really protect? | Opinion
By McClatchy Media’s California editorial board
Updated October 2, 2026 3:35 PM
Prop. 42 would block new state taxes on personal property and limit retroactive taxes, challenging California’s proposed billionaire wealth tax in 2026.
Victorburnside
Getty Images/iStockphoto
The backers ofProposition 42 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/42/index.htm) want voters to believe it is needed to prevent state legislators from raiding the retirement accounts of everyday Californians.
But the principal backers of Prop. 42 are billionaires seeking to avoid higher taxes and thwartProposition 40 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article316881754.html), the controversial ballot measure that would impose a one-time wealth tax on California’s richest residents.
Prop. 42 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/article317007039.html) is one of two ballot measures that could derail Prop. 40. The other isProposition 41. (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317122476.html) Under the California Constitution, when two measures approved in the same election conflict, the one receiving more affirmative votes prevails. Thus, if either Prop. 42 or Prop. 41 receives more yes votes than Prop. 40, the one-time 5 percent wealth tax on Californians with more than $1 billion in assets, would not take effect.
THE BEE’S VOTER GUIDE: Your guide to Proposition 42 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/article317007039.html)
At its core, Prop. 42 is presented as a safeguard for personal property and 401(k) accounts. If approved, it would bar new state taxes on those assets, though its real purpose is to shield billionaires from the tax proposed by Prop. 40.
The suggestion that any governor who would raid the modest retirement nest eggs or property of middle-class Californians is crazy because that governor would soon be unemployed for trying. Even the left-leaning state Legislature, which enjoys spending more than it should, knows not to mess with your 401(k).
Prop. 42 purports to address a problem that does not exist. It would prohibit new state taxes (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop42-text-proposed-laws.pdf) on personal property—including retirement accounts, savings, investments and business interests—and restrict certain retroactive taxes. The measure would embed those limits in the California Constitution, leaving voters as the only route to change them.
Even without Prop. 40 on the ballot, Prop. 42 would create the illusion of permanently settling California tax policy on financial assets and other personal property. In fact, it would restrict the state’s future options for taxing those assets, while a later constitutional amendment or competing voter-approved measure could still alter that policy.
Opponents claim that it is illegal to tax retirement accounts such as 401(k)s. This appears to be an unsettled legal issue (https://www.irs.gov/retirement-plans/irc-403b-tax-sheltered-annuity-plans) because no government has been reckless enough to try. To assert that a constitutional amendment is necessary to protect the nest eggs of every-day Californians is beyond overreach.
Proposition 40 squarely voters with a question: Should California impose a one-timewealth tax on roughly 200 residents with net worth above $1 billion? (https://www.businessinsider.com/california-billionaires-list-wealth-tax-2026-1) Prop. 42 exists to undermine that choice and should be judged accordingly—by the interests of the billionaires financing it.
Prop. 42 is a poison pill designed to derail the real debate over a one-time wealth tax on billionaires. Voters should reject the decoy and vote no.

# Taxing wealth is a dangerous step toward taxing retirement savings
This November, Californians have an opportunity to protect the hard-earned retirement savings they have earned.
For the workers I represent, retirement isn’t a windfall.
It’s earned across jobsites from thousands of hours worked, over decades of early mornings, long shifts and hard physical work.
We need to protect what we’ve saved — and that’s why I’m voting yes on Proposition 42.
Working people already pay income taxes on the money they earn.
They shouldn’t pay taxes on that money twice simply because it’s sitting in a retirement or savings account.
Proposition 42 prevents that double taxation by closing a loophole in California’s Constitution that allows new taxes to be imposed on retirement accounts, life savings and other personal property.

Proposition 42 says it protects your 401(k). Who does it really protect? | Opinion
By McClatchy Media’s California editorial board
Updated October 2, 2026 3:35 PM
Prop. 42 would block new state taxes on personal property and limit retroactive taxes, challenging California’s proposed billionaire wealth tax in 2026.
Victorburnside
Getty Images/iStockphoto
The backers ofProposition 42 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/42/index.htm) want voters to believe it is needed to prevent state legislators from raiding the retirement accounts of everyday Californians.
But the principal backers of Prop. 42 are billionaires seeking to avoid higher taxes and thwartProposition 40 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article316881754.html), the controversial ballot measure that would impose a one-time wealth tax on California’s richest residents.
Prop. 42 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/article317007039.html) is one of two ballot measures that could derail Prop. 40. The other isProposition 41. (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317122476.html) Under the California Constitution, when two measures approved in the same election conflict, the one receiving more affirmative votes prevails. Thus, if either Prop. 42 or Prop. 41 receives more yes votes than Prop. 40, the one-time 5 percent wealth tax on Californians with more than $1 billion in assets, would not take effect.
THE BEE’S VOTER GUIDE: Your guide to Proposition 42 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/article317007039.html)
At its core, Prop. 42 is presented as a safeguard for personal property and 401(k) accounts. If approved, it would bar new state taxes on those assets, though its real purpose is to shield billionaires from the tax proposed by Prop. 40.
The suggestion that any governor who would raid the modest retirement nest eggs or property of middle-class Californians is crazy because that governor would soon be unemployed for trying. Even the left-leaning state Legislature, which enjoys spending more than it should, knows not to mess with your 401(k).
Prop. 42 purports to address a problem that does not exist. It would prohibit new state taxes (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop42-text-proposed-laws.pdf) on personal property—including retirement accounts, savings, investments and business interests—and restrict certain retroactive taxes. The measure would embed those limits in the California Constitution, leaving voters as the only route to change them.
Even without Prop. 40 on the ballot, Prop. 42 would create the illusion of permanently settling California tax policy on financial assets and other personal property. In fact, it would restrict the state’s future options for taxing those assets, while a later constitutional amendment or competing voter-approved measure could still alter that policy.
Opponents claim that it is illegal to tax retirement accounts such as 401(k)s. This appears to be an unsettled legal issue (https://www.irs.gov/retirement-plans/irc-403b-tax-sheltered-annuity-plans) because no government has been reckless enough to try. To assert that a constitutional amendment is necessary to protect the nest eggs of every-day Californians is beyond overreach.
Proposition 40 squarely voters with a question: Should California impose a one-timewealth tax on roughly 200 residents with net worth above $1 billion? (https://www.businessinsider.com/california-billionaires-list-wealth-tax-2026-1) Prop. 42 exists to undermine that choice and should be judged accordingly—by the interests of the billionaires financing it.
Prop. 42 is a poison pill designed to derail the real debate over a one-time wealth tax on billionaires. Voters should reject the decoy and vote no.

Proposition 42 says it protects your 401(k). Who does it really protect? | Opinion
By McClatchy Media’s California editorial board
Updated October 2, 2026 3:35 PM
Prop. 42 would block new state taxes on personal property and limit retroactive taxes, challenging California’s proposed billionaire wealth tax in 2026.
Victorburnside
Getty Images/iStockphoto
The backers ofProposition 42 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/42/index.htm) want voters to believe it is needed to prevent state legislators from raiding the retirement accounts of everyday Californians.
But the principal backers of Prop. 42 are billionaires seeking to avoid higher taxes and thwartProposition 40 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article316881754.html), the controversial ballot measure that would impose a one-time wealth tax on California’s richest residents.
Prop. 42 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/article317007039.html) is one of two ballot measures that could derail Prop. 40. The other isProposition 41. (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317122476.html) Under the California Constitution, when two measures approved in the same election conflict, the one receiving more affirmative votes prevails. Thus, if either Prop. 42 or Prop. 41 receives more yes votes than Prop. 40, the one-time 5 percent wealth tax on Californians with more than $1 billion in assets, would not take effect.
THE BEE’S VOTER GUIDE: Your guide to Proposition 42 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/article317007039.html)
At its core, Prop. 42 is presented as a safeguard for personal property and 401(k) accounts. If approved, it would bar new state taxes on those assets, though its real purpose is to shield billionaires from the tax proposed by Prop. 40.
The suggestion that any governor who would raid the modest retirement nest eggs or property of middle-class Californians is crazy because that governor would soon be unemployed for trying. Even the left-leaning state Legislature, which enjoys spending more than it should, knows not to mess with your 401(k).
Prop. 42 purports to address a problem that does not exist. It would prohibit new state taxes (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop42-text-proposed-laws.pdf) on personal property—including retirement accounts, savings, investments and business interests—and restrict certain retroactive taxes. The measure would embed those limits in the California Constitution, leaving voters as the only route to change them.
Even without Prop. 40 on the ballot, Prop. 42 would create the illusion of permanently settling California tax policy on financial assets and other personal property. In fact, it would restrict the state’s future options for taxing those assets, while a later constitutional amendment or competing voter-approved measure could still alter that policy.
Opponents claim that it is illegal to tax retirement accounts such as 401(k)s. This appears to be an unsettled legal issue (https://www.irs.gov/retirement-plans/irc-403b-tax-sheltered-annuity-plans) because no government has been reckless enough to try. To assert that a constitutional amendment is necessary to protect the nest eggs of every-day Californians is beyond overreach.
Proposition 40 squarely voters with a question: Should California impose a one-timewealth tax on roughly 200 residents with net worth above $1 billion? (https://www.businessinsider.com/california-billionaires-list-wealth-tax-2026-1) Prop. 42 exists to undermine that choice and should be judged accordingly—by the interests of the billionaires financing it.
Prop. 42 is a poison pill designed to derail the real debate over a one-time wealth tax on billionaires. Voters should reject the decoy and vote no.

Proposition 42 says it protects your 401(k). Who does it really protect? | Opinion
By McClatchy Media’s California editorial board
Updated October 2, 2026 3:35 PM
Prop. 42 would block new state taxes on personal property and limit retroactive taxes, challenging California’s proposed billionaire wealth tax in 2026.
Victorburnside
Getty Images/iStockphoto
The backers ofProposition 42 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/42/index.htm) want voters to believe it is needed to prevent state legislators from raiding the retirement accounts of everyday Californians.
But the principal backers of Prop. 42 are billionaires seeking to avoid higher taxes and thwartProposition 40 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article316881754.html), the controversial ballot measure that would impose a one-time wealth tax on California’s richest residents.
Prop. 42 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/article317007039.html) is one of two ballot measures that could derail Prop. 40. The other isProposition 41. (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317122476.html) Under the California Constitution, when two measures approved in the same election conflict, the one receiving more affirmative votes prevails. Thus, if either Prop. 42 or Prop. 41 receives more yes votes than Prop. 40, the one-time 5 percent wealth tax on Californians with more than $1 billion in assets, would not take effect.
THE BEE’S VOTER GUIDE: Your guide to Proposition 42 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/article317007039.html)
At its core, Prop. 42 is presented as a safeguard for personal property and 401(k) accounts. If approved, it would bar new state taxes on those assets, though its real purpose is to shield billionaires from the tax proposed by Prop. 40.
The suggestion that any governor who would raid the modest retirement nest eggs or property of middle-class Californians is crazy because that governor would soon be unemployed for trying. Even the left-leaning state Legislature, which enjoys spending more than it should, knows not to mess with your 401(k).
Prop. 42 purports to address a problem that does not exist. It would prohibit new state taxes (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop42-text-proposed-laws.pdf) on personal property—including retirement accounts, savings, investments and business interests—and restrict certain retroactive taxes. The measure would embed those limits in the California Constitution, leaving voters as the only route to change them.
Even without Prop. 40 on the ballot, Prop. 42 would create the illusion of permanently settling California tax policy on financial assets and other personal property. In fact, it would restrict the state’s future options for taxing those assets, while a later constitutional amendment or competing voter-approved measure could still alter that policy.
Opponents claim that it is illegal to tax retirement accounts such as 401(k)s. This appears to be an unsettled legal issue (https://www.irs.gov/retirement-plans/irc-403b-tax-sheltered-annuity-plans) because no government has been reckless enough to try. To assert that a constitutional amendment is necessary to protect the nest eggs of every-day Californians is beyond overreach.
Proposition 40 squarely voters with a question: Should California impose a one-timewealth tax on roughly 200 residents with net worth above $1 billion? (https://www.businessinsider.com/california-billionaires-list-wealth-tax-2026-1) Prop. 42 exists to undermine that choice and should be judged accordingly—by the interests of the billionaires financing it.
Prop. 42 is a poison pill designed to derail the real debate over a one-time wealth tax on billionaires. Voters should reject the decoy and vote no.

Now I have a comprehensive picture. Let me also quickly note some final considerations and check one more angle — the legal/scholarly analysis of Prop 42's potential broader consequences (e.g., threat to health plan/hospital taxes that fund Medi-Cal mentioned in the TaxProf Blog op-ed). That's about Prop 41 mostly ("threats to the health plan and hospital taxes"). Let me quickly check the Grant Thornton analysis and the californiatoday.com guide for the funding details, and possibly the TaxProf Blog piece. Actually, I have enough on the core. Let me do one final check on who the other funders are and the overall funding totals, plus the California Democratic Party's stance (they endorsed Prop 40 and oppose 41/42 per the LA Times article — confirmed: "The party also voted to oppose two competing ballot measures that seek to undercut the billionaire tax").

Summary of the research:

**What Prop 42 does (per official LAO/voter guide):**
- Constitutional amendment (initiative) titled "Retirement and Personal Savings Protection Act of 2026."
- Prohibits any new state tax on the ownership/control of "retirement holdings, individually owned assets, and other forms of personal savings" — defined to include ALL personal property, tangible or intangible (pensions, 401(k)s, IRAs, mutual funds, stocks, business interests, digital assets, IP, personal belongings).
- Applies to state laws and constitutional provisions enacted on/after Jan 1, 2026 — i.e., retroactively nullifying Prop 40 if Prop 40 passes with fewer votes.
- Prohibits retroactive taxes (including taxes based on prior residency status) — with a narrow exception only for legislative statutes (not initiatives) with ≤365 days retroactivity during declared emergencies/fiscal emergencies with dedicated revenue.
- Poison pill: if it gets more votes than a conflicting measure (Prop 40), ALL provisions of the conflicting measure are null and void.
- LAO fiscal impact: possibility that future revenues will be lower; unclear by how much.

**Context:**
- Prop 40 (same ballot): one-time 5% wealth tax on ~200-250 billionaires who were CA residents on Jan 1, 2026; real estate, pensions, retirement accounts excluded (except mega-Roth >$10M counted); 90% of revenue to healthcare amid ~$100B federal Medicaid cuts; drafted with Berkeley economists (Saez/Zucman); sponsored by SEIU-UHW; endorsed by CA Democratic Party, Bernie Sanders; opposed by Newsom, LA Times editorial (the LAT editorial board situation is murky — per TaxProf Blog, LAT has no functioning editorial board since 2025); PPIC Oct poll: 46% yes/52% no.
- Prop 42 funded by Building a Better California — $100M+ from Sergey Brin (who moved to Nevada in 2025), plus other tech billionaires (L. John Doerr, etc.); total ~$112.8M, the largest ballot-measure campaign this cycle. Brin's personal stake: ~$12-13B.
- Newsom endorsed Yes on 42 (Oct 9).
- California Democratic Party opposes 42; CA Professional Firefighters, State Building & Construction Trades Council, PORAC, AMVETS, CA Small Business Assn, CA Senior Alliance support.

**Editorial/independent positions on Prop 42:**
- SF Chronicle: NO ("poison pill," "appalling tactic"; "no one is coming for your 401(k)"; six wealth tax bills all died; retroactivity ban unnecessary and legally messy vs. Carlton).
- Mercury News/East Bay Times: NO (even though they oppose Prop 40 — "If this initiative had limited itself to nullifying Proposition 40, we could have supported it. However... California must keep its options open. This measure would needlessly and recklessly narrow them.")
- McClatchy/Sacramento Bee CA editorial board: NO ("poison pill," "the 401(k) decoy," "purports to address a problem that does not exist"). (The one "✅ Yes on 42" I saw was likely an individual's pick in their multi-voice roundup; the McClatchy CA editorial board itself says vote no. Wait — result 6 in an earlier search said "✅ Yes on Prop 42" in the Sac Bee opinion team's cheat sheet. Hmm, that's inconsistent with their Oct 1 editorial "Voters should reject the decoy and vote no." The cheat sheet link (article317708656) might aggregate individual columnists' picks rather than the board's; or the board may have changed. The dedicated editorial article (article317166989) is clearly the board's position: "Voters should reject the decoy and vote no." I'll trust that. Either way, the dominant editorial view is No.)
- George Skelton (LA Times veteran columnist): NO on both 41 and 42 ("twin poison pills," deceptive games-playing) — while also opposing Prop 40.
- Daily Californian editorial board: NO on 41/42.
- The Atlantic: harshly critical ("deviously cynical electoral maneuver," plutocrats capturing the ballot-measure process).
- Forbes (Ghilarducci, labor economist): critical ("labels run backward").
- TaxProf Blog (law professors Galle et al.): even principled opponents of Prop 40 should vote against 41/42 because they undermine democracy and could have unforeseen consequences (threats to health plan/hospital taxes that fund Medi-Cal).
- CalMatters reporting: notes Brin funding, and CBPC analyst noting the retroactivity ban removes anti-avoidance tools.
- Grant Thornton (neutral tax firm): explains the interplay — 41/42 "designed to block" 40.

**The Yes case:**
- Protects retirement/personal savings from future wealth taxes; "double taxation" argument.
- Bans retroactive taxes (fairness).
- Newsom's argument: wealth tax would drive billionaires away, hurting revenue.
- Supporters: firefighter/ building trades/ police unions (whose pensions are the ostensible concern), veterans, small business, seniors.
- The genuine kernel: legislators HAVE introduced wealth tax bills (AB 2088 in 2020: 0.4% annual tax on net worth > $30M; AB 259 in 2023-24 with ACA 3; and others) — all died. So the concept isn't hypothetical, though none targeted ordinary retirement accounts.

**Counterpoints to the Yes case:**
- No one is proposing to tax ordinary retirement accounts; Prop 40 excludes them (except mega-Roths >$10M, a billionaire phenomenon); CA follows the federal framework (tax on withdrawal).

The dedicated editorial article (article317166989) is clearly the board's position: "Voters should reject the decoy and vote no." I'll trust that. Either way, the dominant editorial view is No.)
- George Skelton (LA Times veteran columnist): NO on both 41 and 42 ("twin poison pills," deceptive games-playing) — while also opposing Prop 40.
- Daily Californian editorial board: NO on 41/42.
- The Atlantic: harshly critical ("deviously cynical electoral maneuver," plutocrats capturing the ballot-measure process).
- Forbes (Ghilarducci, labor economist): critical ("labels run backward").
- TaxProf Blog (law professors Galle et al.): even principled opponents of Prop 40 should vote against 41/42 because they undermine democracy and could have unforeseen consequences (threats to health plan/hospital taxes that fund Medi-Cal).
- CalMatters reporting: notes Brin funding, and CBPC analyst noting the retroactivity ban removes anti-avoidance tools.
- Grant Thornton (neutral tax firm): explains the interplay — 41/42 "designed to block" 40.

**The Yes case:**
- Protects retirement/personal savings from future wealth taxes; "double taxation" argument.
- Bans retroactive taxes (fairness).
- Newsom's argument: wealth tax would drive billionaires away, hurting revenue.
- Supporters: firefighter/ building trades/ police unions (whose pensions are the ostensible concern), veterans, small business, seniors.
- The genuine kernel: legislators HAVE introduced wealth tax bills (AB 2088 in 2020: 0.4% annual tax on net worth > $30M; AB 259 in 2023-24 with ACA 3; and others) — all died. So the concept isn't hypothetical, though none targeted ordinary retirement accounts.

**Counterpoints to the Yes case:**
- No one is proposing to tax ordinary retirement accounts; Prop 40 excludes them (except mega-Roths >$10M, a billionaire phenomenon); CA follows the federal framework (tax on withdrawal).
- The "double taxation" framing is misleading: traditional 401(k)/IRA contributions are pre-tax (money in them has NOT been taxed yet); the state taxes income when realized.
- All six wealth tax proposals since 2019 died without passing.
- The measure is engineered as a poison pill: it would nullify Prop 40 even if Prop 40 passes with majority support; the emergency exception deliberately excludes initiatives (the vehicle used for Prop 40).
- It permanently bans ANY state personal-property tax with no emergency exception at all, locking detailed tax policy into the constitution and foreclosing future options (this is why even Prop 40 opponents like the Mercury News and Skelton oppose 42).
- Funded overwhelmingly by billionaires with a direct $12B+ stake (Brin, who already moved to Nevada).
- The retroactivity ban conflicts with the U.S. Supreme Court's Carlton standard and could create legal complications for routine tax administration.

**My decision:** No.

Reasoning: Even setting aside one's view of the billionaire tax (Prop 40), Prop 42 is a deceptively marketed, overbroad constitutional amendment whose core purpose is to nullify a rival measure through a poison-pill mechanism. Its central selling point — protecting ordinary retirement savings from double taxation — addresses a threat that doesn't exist under current law or any live proposal (Prop 40 itself exempts retirement accounts and pensions). Meanwhile, its real effects are to: (1) permanently entrench in the state constitution an absolute ban on any future state personal-property tax (with no emergency exception), foreclosing future democratic choices in a period of major fiscal/AI-driven uncertainty; (2) impose a retroactivity ban that clashes with settled federal constitutional doctrine and standard anti-avoidance tools; and (3) enable an antimajoritarian outcome where a majority votes for the wealth tax but it dies anyway. The overwhelming majority of independent editorial assessments — including boards that OPPOSE the billionaire tax itself (Mercury News/East Bay Times, SF Chronicle, George Skelton/LA Times) — recommend No precisely because of this deceptive design and overreach. The Yes side's case rests on fear-mongering about retirement accounts that is not grounded in any actual proposal, and its funding is dominated by a single billionaire who would personally save ~$12 billion and has already moved out of the state.

There is a genuine ideological case for banning wealth taxes, and some credible figures (Newsom) support 42 on those grounds. But as a matter of the measure itself — its honesty, drafting, breadth, and process — the better vote is No. Also substantively: even if one opposes wealth taxes, a cleaner way to express that is to vote No on Prop 40 itself; voting Yes on 42 rewards the poison-pill tactic and enshrines an overbroad, inflexible constitutional ban.

assistantMessageEvent.content:
Now I have the complete picture of organizational alignments:

**Support Prop 42:** California Republican Party, Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, Reform California, NAACP CA/Hawaii, California Taxpayers Association, CA Chamber of Commerce, CA Professional Firefighters, State Building & Construction Trades Council, PORAC, AMVETS, CA Small Business Assn, CA Senior Alliance, Gov. Gavin Newsom, Building a Better California (Brin et al.)

**Oppose Prop 42:** California Democratic Party, SEIU-UHW, Bernie Sanders, Berkeley Political Review, editorial boards of SF Chronicle, Mercury News/East Bay Times, McClatchy/Sac Bee CA editorial board, Daily Californian, George Skelton (LA Times).

Now let me make my final determination.

Weighing everything:

**The case for Yes:**
1. Ideological/taxpayer view: permanently ban wealth taxes in CA constitution; HJTA/CAGOP support; protect against legislature's recurring wealth tax proposals (AB 2088, AB 259 all introduced, though all died).
2. Ban on retroactive taxes has intuitive fairness appeal.
3. Newsom's endorsement and concern about billionaire flight.
4. Voters who oppose Prop 40 but fear it passing could use 42 as a backstop.

**The case for No:**
1. **Deceptive design**: Marketed as protecting retirement savings ("Retirement and Personal Savings Protection Act") when its actual primary function is a poison pill to nullify Prop 40 — the billionaire tax — even if a majority of voters approve Prop 40. The emergency exception is deliberately limited to legislative statutes, excluding initiatives (the vehicle of Prop 40), revealing the tailored intent.
2. **Nonexistent problem**: No live proposal taxes ordinary retirement accounts. CA follows the federal model (tax on withdrawal, not deposit). Prop 40 itself excludes pensions and retirement accounts. All six wealth tax bills since 2019 died in the legislature. The "double taxation" argument is misleading (traditional 401(k)/IRA money is pre-tax and untaxed until withdrawal).
3. **Overbreadth and constitutional lock-in**: It would permanently ban ANY new state personal-property tax with no exceptions whatsoever, in an era of fiscal and technological uncertainty — even editorial boards that OPPOSE the billionaire tax (Mercury News/East Bay Times: "If this initiative had limited itself to nullifying Proposition 40, we could have supported it. PROP
42
PROHIBITS NEW STATE PERSONAL PROPERTY TAXES AND CERTAIN RETROACTIVE STATE TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Prohibits any new state tax (1) imposed on the ownership of personal property (all things people own other than real estate), or (2) that applies retroactively based on taxpayer’s past activities. Nullifies taxes enacted after January 1, 2026 that conflict with this measure. Fiscal Impact: Possibility that tax revenues will not go up as much in the future. Supporters: CA Professional Firefighters; State Building & Construction Trades Council of CA; AMVETS Department of CA Opponents: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: The state could not establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would continue to have the option to establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
California’s Constitution currently allows the Legislature to tax retirement and savings—even though you already paid taxes on that money when you earned it! Prop. 42 protects Californians from this double taxation, by prohibiting new and retroactive taxes on personal property, including retirement and savings. You earned it. Prop. 42 protects it.
CON
This is just another billionaire-funded trick. Prop. 42 isn’t really about protecting your retirement savings—its only real purpose is to undo the California Billionaire Tax. Billionaires would rather millions of Californians lose healthcare than pay a modest tax on their extreme wealth. Vote NO on 42.

PROHIBITS NEW STATE PERSONAL PROPERTY TAXES AND CERTAIN RETROACTIVE STATE TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
Certain Personal Property Is Taxed in California. Both the state and local governments tax the ownership of certain personal property. These taxes are based on the property’s value. Personal property is all the things that people own other than real estate. One example of these kinds of taxes is the vehicle license fee that car and truck owners pay to the Department of Motor Vehicles each year. Another example is the property taxes owners of business equipment pay to the county each year.
Ownership of Financial Assets Is Not Taxed. The ownership of many types of personal property is not taxed. One major example is financial assets like stocks and investment accounts. Although the state does tax income people make from their financial assets, there is no tax for simply owning those assets.
PROPOSAL
Prohibits New Taxes on Financial Assets or Other Personal Property. Under Proposition 42, new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property would not be allowed.
Limits Retroactive Taxes. Proposition 42 limits the situations that a ballot measure or the Legislature can raise any tax retroactively. A retroactive tax is one that applies to things that happened in the past. An example is a tax on money someone earned two years ago.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Possibility That Tax Revenues Will Be Lower in the Future. Proposition 42 restricts the options the state has to raise taxes in the future. This could make it somewhat harder for the state to raise taxes. This could reduce future tax revenues. When and by how much future revenues would be reduced is unclear.

PROP
42
PROHIBITS NEW STATE PERSONAL PROPERTY TAXES AND CERTAIN RETROACTIVE STATE TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 42
YES ON PROP. 42: PROTECT YOUR RETIREMENT AND LIFE SAVINGS FROM STATE TAXES
California is now the third most expensive state to retire in the nation. Every year, higher costs and taxes make it harder to save. An April 2026 survey found 73% of Californians know someone who has had to delay retirement for financial reasons.
CALIFORNIA CONSTITUTION CURRENTLY ALLOWS DOUBLE TAXATION
Yet, California’s Constitution currently allows the Legislature to tax the value of our personal property like retirement funds and savings accounts, even though residents already pay income tax on that money when they earn it. This means politicians can tax the same money twice: once when you earn it, and again when it is sitting in your retirement funds or savings accounts. That’s double taxation!
In the last few years alone, the Legislature and special interests have introduced six separate proposals that would tax retirement and savings accounts.
Taxes and cost of living are already too high in California-we need protections against taxes on our personal property and retirement savings.
PROP. 42 PROHIBITS TAXES ON RETIREMENT AND SAVINGS
Prop. 42 amends the state Constitution to protect Californians from this double taxation by special interests and politicians. Specifically, the measure:
• Prohibits new taxes on personal property, such as retirement funds, pensions and savings accounts; • Prohibits retroactive taxes; and • Prohibits all new taxes on retirement and savings this year and in the future.
PROP. 42 PROTECTS ALL FORMS OF RETIREMENT FUNDS AND SAVINGS FROM NEW TAXES
Roughly 80% of Californians report having some form of retirement fund or savings, including young workers just beginning to save; teachers, firefighters and police officers with pensions; and retirees who depend on their savings for financial security.
This measure protects all forms of personal property from new taxes, including 401ks, pensions, IRAs and personal savings.
“Prop. 42 protects Californians’ savings and retirement. Whether it’s a union member’s hard-earned pension or a small business owner’s IRA, new taxes on retirement shouldn’t stand between people and the security they’ve planned for.” -Chris Hannan, President, State Building and Construction Trades Council of California representing hundreds of thousands of union construction trades workers.
PROP. 42 PROHIBITS UNFAIR RETROACTIVE TAXES
The state should not be able to pass new taxes that apply retroactively to money that taxpayers earned in the past. Prop. 42 requires any new taxes to apply only after voters have approved them.
“It’s a question of fairness and common sense. People plan their retirement for years-they deserve stable, predictable rules that don’t change after years of saving and planning. Prop. 42 provides that certainty.” -Sean Morgan, licensed financial advisor
Prop. 42 is supported by a broad coalition of seniors, veterans, small business owners, blue-collar workers, retirees, including groups like the California Professional Firefighters and Disabled American Veterans, Dept. of California.
Californians are already struggling with high costs of living and high taxes. Many work their entire lives to achieve some measure of retirement security. It should be illegal for politicians and special interests to tax our retirement and savings.
You earned and saved it. Now we need to protect it. Please join us in voting Yes on 42. YesonProp42.org
Michael Hedges , President
California Small Business Association
Shelley Huff , Commander
AMVETS, Department of California
Jennifer Yoder , Board Member
California Senior Alliance
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 42
THIS IS ANOTHER BILLIONAIRE-FUNDED TRICK
Don’t be fooled-Prop. 42 is not really about protecting your retirement savings from new taxes.
It’s a redundant, expensive trick to allow approximately 200 billionaires to keep avoiding paying their own taxes while YOU get stuck with the bill.
PROP. 42 WOULD CANCEL OUT THE BILLIONAIRE TAX
Prop. 42 is a billionaire-funded scheme designed specifically to undo the California Billionaire Tax, Prop. 40.
Prop. 42 was put on the ballot because billionaires don’t want to pay their fair share. They’d rather millions of working people lose healthcare than pay a modest, one-time tax on their extreme wealth.
WHO’S BEHIND THIS? SOME OF DONALD TRUMP’S DONORS
The billionaires behind this don’t care about protecting your retirement savings. They’re protecting themselves. They’ve been getting out of paying their own taxes for years through loopholes and tax breaks.
This sham initiative was created to trick voters like you into making a billionaire tax impossible to enforce. That’s why you must vote NO.
PROP. 40 WOULD ONLY TAX BILLIONAIRES’ $2 TRILLION IN WEALTH
The billionaires behind Prop. 42 have spread lies about the California Billionaire Tax (Prop. 40), trying to trick voters into thinking that their retirement and savings are at risk.
Don’t buy the fear-mongering. The California Billionaires Tax ONLY applies to billionaires. It’s about making billionaires finally pay their fair share so we’re not stuck with shuttered hospitals and skyrocketing healthcare costs.
Vote NO on Prop. 42.
Suzanne Jimenez , Chief of Staff
SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West
ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 42
VOTE NO ON PROP. 42. This is a billionaire-funded initiative designed specifically to undo the California Billionaire Tax, Prop. 40.
PROP. 42 WOULD CANCEL OUT THE BILLIONAIRE TAX
Prop. 42 was put on the ballot for one reason-because billionaires don’t want to pay their fair share. This initiative was created to trick voters like you into making a billionaire tax impossible to enforce. That’s why you must vote NO.
Don’t fall for the billionaires’ lies. Prop. 42 isn’t about preventing new taxes on personal property. It’s about preventing one specific tax that billionaires want to avoid, because they’d rather millions of working people lose healthcare than pay a modest, one-time tax on their extreme wealth.
PROP. 42 WAS FUNDED BY BILLIONAIRES WHO WANT YOU TO PAY MORE FOR HEALTHCARE
One of Prop. 42’s main funders is Google founder and Trump donor Sergey Brin, whose wealth has DOUBLED to nearly $300 billion since Trump’s election. Now he’s spent over $57 million to fund sham measures like Prop. 42 that attempt to cancel out a billionaire tax. U.S. Senator Bernie Sanders called this arrogant move by Brin “unacceptable.”
Donald Trump took money out of working peoples’ pockets and gave it to billionaires like Brin through massive tax breaks. Now, the billionaires backing Prop. 42 want YOU to pay more for your healthcare.
VOTE NO ON PROP. 42 IF YOU SUPPORT THE BILLIONAIRE TAX
We have a chance to make billionaires pay their fair share to keep hospitals open and healthcare affordable for California’s working families. Vote NO on Prop. 42.
Suzanne Jimenez , Chief of Staff
SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT AGAINST
PROPOSITION 42
WHO SUPPORTS PROP. 42
Prop. 42 is supported by hundreds of thousands of seniors, veterans, firefighters, blue-collar workers, public-safety officers and working families because it protects the retirement and savings of ALL Californians from new taxes. Who opposes 42? One organization that wants to tax retirement accounts.
WHY WE NEED PROP. 42
Sacramento politicians and special interests have repeatedly tried to pass taxes on retirement and personal savings accounts in recent years. They’ve relied on a loophole in California’s Constitution that allows government to tax our income when we earn it, and AGAIN when it is simply sitting in our savings and retirement accounts.
CALIFORNIA IS EXPENSIVE ENOUGH WITHOUT DOUBLE TAXATION
Prop. 42 prohibits this double taxation by PROHIBITING ALL NEW TAXES ON RETIREMENT AND SAVINGS ACCOUNTS and other personal property, whether proposed by legislation or ballot measure, including proposals on this year’s ballot and in the future.
It is a comprehensive constitutional protection against politicians or special interests trying to tax our retirement funds and savings accounts.
WHO BENEFITS FROM PROP. 42
Prop. 42 protects the retirement and savings for all Californians-young workers just beginning to save; teachers, firefighters and police officers with pensions; retirees and veterans who depend on their savings for financial security.
You saved it. You deserve to keep it.
Prop. 42 asks a simple question: should California politicians have the power to tax your personal property, including retirement and savings accounts?
If you think your retirement and savings should be protected from taxes, vote Yes on 42.
Darrell Roberts , President
California Professional Firefighters
Chris Hannan , President
State Building and Construction Trades Council of California
Brian R. Marvel , President
Peace Officers Research Association of California

# Proposition 42
Prohibits New State Personal Property Taxes and Certain Retroactive State Taxes.
Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
## Analysis of Measure
### Background
***Certain Personal Property Is Taxed in California.*** Both the state and local governments tax the ownership of certain personal property.
These taxes are based on the property’s value.
Personal property is all the things that people own other than real estate.
One example of these kinds of taxes is the vehicle license fee that car and truck owners pay to the Department of Motor Vehicles each year.
Another example is the property taxes owners of business equipment pay to the county each year.
***Ownership of Financial Assets Is Not Taxed.*** The ownership of many types of personal property is not taxed.
One major example is financial assets like stocks and investment accounts.
Although the state does tax income people make from their financial assets, there is no tax for simply owning those assets.
### Proposal
***Prohibits New Taxes on Financial Assets or Other Personal Property.*** Under Proposition 42, new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property would not be allowed.
***Limits Retroactive Taxes.*** Proposition 42 limits the situations that a ballot measure or the Legislature can raise any tax retroactively.
A retroactive tax is one that applies to things that happened in the past.
An example is a tax on money someone earned two years ago.

PROPOSED LAW
SECTION 1. Title.
This act shall be known, and may be cited, as the
Retirement and Personal Savings Protection Act of
2026.
SEC. 2. Findings and Declarations.
(a) California families are paying more for everything
and we already pay some of the highest taxes in the
country. A recent analysis by a nonpartisan research
institute concluded that California ranks 3rd worst in
the nation in subjecting its population to taxes when
considering individual income taxes, sales taxes,
property taxes, and other forms of taxation. California is
behind only New Jersey and the District of Columbia in
this regard. California also has the highest state sales
TEXT OF PROPOSED LAWS PROPOSITION 42 CONTINUED
tax in the nation, the highest top income tax rate, and
the highest tax on gasoline, among other indicators.
(b) Every day, Californians are also facing an
affordability crisis. Costs for housing, food, electricity,
health care, home and auto insurance, and many other
life necessities continue to escalate. Californians are
struggling economically just to make ends meet on a
daily basis. Saving for retirement or a rainy day is even
harder. Given the state’s extraordinarily high cost of
living, a recent analysis suggests that Californians
would need $2.3 million saved up if they want to retire
comfortably for 20 years. This is an impossible sum for
many Californians.
(c) To make matters worse, politicians and special
interest groups want to start taxing retirement holdings,
individually owned assets, and other forms of personal
savings—even though the “California Dream” is getting
further out of reach for many of us and many
Californians struggle to save enough money to retire.
Here is just some of what could be at risk:
(1) Teachers, police officers, firefighters, and other
dedicated workers earn defined-benefit pension
benefits. They could be taxed on the future value of
their pension benefits and forced to pay the
government before they ever collect a dime in pension
pay.
(2) Californians who contribute to 401(k) retirement
plans and individual retirement accounts (IRAs), and
invest in stocks, bonds, mutual funds, and other
investments could be taxed on the value of their
retirement nest eggs. This could cost workers some of
their hard-earned savings, causing them to put off
retirement and leaving them more economically
vulnerable later in life.
(d) California already imposes income taxes, capital
gains taxes, real property taxes, personal property
taxes, corporation taxes, sales and use taxes, real
property transaction taxes and many other taxes on its
residents. In addition, once Californians begin to
access their retirement holdings, sell their individually
owned assets, or realize the growth in other personal
savings, they are already subject to the state’s income,
capital gains, and property taxes. But politicians and
special interests should be prohibited from taxing the
mere ownership or control of personal property such as
retirement holdings, individually owned assets, and
other forms of personal savings that Californians work
hard to save.
(e) Retroactive taxes can have the same devastating
effects on Californians’ retirement planning and
personal savings. Fundamental principles of fairness in
a democratic society require that individuals, families,
and businesses be able to understand and rely upon
the tax laws that govern their financial planning so they
can make decisions with advance notice of what the
rules are.
(f) The ability of Californians to organize and achieve
their financial and retirement goals depends on having
advance notice of the tax obligations that apply to
them. Retroactive changes to tax laws are
fundamentally unfair and undermine confidence in
government, disrupt retirement and financial planning,
and prevent residents and businesses from preparing
for the future.
(g) Sacramento politicians and special interests have
wasted billions of our tax dollars on inefficient and
ineffective programs. But they keep coming back for
more of our money with more tax proposals. They don’t
need to tax our retirement holdings or tax us
retroactively based on past conduct, activities, or
status—they need to deliver better results with what
taxpayers have already given them to spend.
SEC. 3. Statement of Purpose.
In enacting this act, the purpose and intent of the
people of the State of California is to protect
Californians’ ability to save for their futures by
prohibiting the imposition of new taxes on our personal
property, including the ownership or control of
retirement holdings, individually owned assets, and
other forms of personal savings as well as requiring all
new taxes to only apply prospectively.
SEC. 4. Article VIII is added to the California
Constitution, to read:
ARTICLE VIII
SECTION 1. Prohibition on Taxing Retirement Holdings,
Individually Owned Assets, and Other Forms of Personal
Savings
(a) No state law and no provision of this Constitution
enacted on or after January 1, 2026, may enact, create,
impose, or authorize collection of a tax on the ownership
or control of retirement holdings, individually owned
assets, and other forms of personal savings, whether
held directly or indirectly.
(b) Nothing in this section shall alter or limit the
imposition or collection of any tax that was in effect,
imposed, and first collected on or before December 31,
2025.
(c) Nothing in this section shall alter or affect the
taxation of real property as provided in other provisions
of this Constitution.
SEC. 2. Prohibition on Retroactive Taxes
(a) (1) No state law and no provision of this
Constitution enacted on or after January 1, 2026, may
enact, create, impose, or authorize collection of a tax
that operates retroactively to result in tax liability based
on conduct, activities, or a status that occurred or was
present prior to the effective date of the state law or
constitutional provision.
(2) This subdivision also applies to a tax that is imposed
on a taxpayer based upon their residency status on a
date prior to the effective date of the tax.
(b) Nothing in subdivision (a) shall alter or limit the
imposition or collection of any tax that was in effect,
imposed, and first collected on or before December 31,
2025.
